#1739. A very positive record: Luca Pairetto will officiate Milan’s game against Frosinone

Luca Pairetto has been assigned to the game between AC Milan and Frosinone on Sunday evening, which is good news for the Rossoneri.

Ruben Amorim and his men will be looking to make it three consecutive wins against Frosinone, after beating Inter and Genoa before the international break. It might not be such an easy task, though, as admitted by the gaffer himself in his press conference.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

Frosinone have indeed started the season well, currently sitting in sixth place, and they don’t really have anything to lose from their trip to San Siro. Only something to gain, which can always make things tricky for the favourite.

Given the above, as always, Milan will be hoping for good officiating to keep the away side from disrupting the play too much. The Italian Referees Association, also known as AIA, announced the referees for this weekend’s game a few days ago and for the Rossoneri, it will be Luca Pairetto.

The 42-year-old is definitely one of the more experienced referees around, even if he has never reached the heights of some of his colleagues. In any case, he has officiated 12 games involving Milan so far and the record is positive: 9 wins, 2 draws and 1 defeat.

It’s been a while since he last officiated a Milan game, though, as we have to go back to the 2024-25 season. The Rossoneri played Empoli and beat them 2-0, courtesy of goals from Rafael Leao and Santiago Gimenez.

Despite the win, the game wasn’t without controversy. A red card was not given to Empoli despite a reckless challenge, and Fikayo Tomori was then given a second yellow when the whole sequence should have been stopped due to offside.

However, most of those errors were made by VAR or the assistant referee and not Pairetto himself.

#1738. 'We felt like medieval peasants coming up against a king': Insiders relive the battle to rid Blackpool of the Oystons, from tangerines stuffed in knickers to a bright orange GTI - and why 'insider dealing' claims mean club isn't out of the woods yet

Published: 07:55 EST, 17 November 2026 | Updated: 18:12 EST, 17 November 2026

In the south London pub where they are readying themselves for a League One match with AFC Wimbledon, Blackpool fans who fought for their club’s heart and soul, 10 years ago, receive a message informing them that half the squad have gone down with a sickness bug so severe that the starting XI will be very unusual.

Three players are too ill to leave the team hotel, the goalkeeper selected is yet to feature in the league this season and the EFL don’t consider this predicament serious enough to cancel the game. The club are already on a run of five defeats in seven.

Moments like this reveal the Blackpool fanbase’s deep sense of perspective, born of their long and often wretched fight to kick out one of British football’s most detested owners, Owen Oyston.

‘We’re still here and we’re watching our club home and away,’ says Andy Higgins, chair of the Blackpool Supporters Trust. ‘We have a good relationship with the club,’ says his friend Dave Ragozzino, with Higgins in the Earlsfield pub. ‘The club are asking us to tell fans what’s going on, and they know we will help. Ten years ago, our club’s owners were suing us.’

The story of the campaign which brought these fans and many more together is told in a superb new documentary The Battle for Blackpool, which screens this week, capturing its spirit, imagination and intelligence.

Oyston and his son Karl have both cooperated with the documentary-makers. Oyston Snr, wearing dark shades and his trademark fedora, is interviewed at his stately home in the Forest of Bowland, while his son Karl, clearly still consumed with hate and contempt for fans, is filmed clay pigeon shooting across their estate.

Blackpool fans watch their team fall to another League One defeat, at AFC Wimbledon on Saturday

The Tangerines are just two points above the relegation zone having lost five out of their last seven league fixtures

Their supporters fought a long and wretched battle against the club's former owner Owen Oyston (pictured in 2017)

The film’s stars are the supporters who led the fight – Christine Seddon, Tim Fielding, Ragozzino, two fans in a Mk1 tangerine Golf GTI and twin sisters of advancing years who embraced the campaign’s guerilla tactics.

Oyston Jr, who chaired the club at his mother’s request after his father was jailed for rape in 1996, tells the documentary-makers: ‘My father likes football. I didn’t.’

It was after he’d stumbled on a managerial genius in Ian Holloway, who took the club into the Premier League for a season in 2010-11, that a full sense of the family’s greed and entitlement became clear.

The Mail on Sunday's Nick Harris revealed that Oyston Snr had paid himself £11million out of the Premier League jackpot, while critics say virtually all the club appeared to get out of promotion was a new sprinkler system. The fight against the Oystons took hold. The Blackpool Supporters Trust, then chaired by Fielding, was its strategic and political wing, flanked by the imaginative sabotage activities of the Tangerine Knights group.

A plot to smuggle tennis balls into the ground for a home match against Burnley, in April 2014, and collectively throw them on the pitch, provides one of the documentary’s many glorious sections. Fans stuffed the missiles into their pants, socks and bras.

‘I had them in my knickers,’ says Christine Atkinson, who is interviewed with her twin sister, Pauline O’Rourke. ‘I didn’t have tennis balls. I had tangerines. It was softer. Less uncomfortable!’

The family of Karl Oyston mocked the tennis ball protest on social media. But it was when his father began suing ordinary fans, some pensioners, for criticising him that the protest escalated.

‘My father created a whole department, scouring message boards full-time so he could sue them,’ Oyston Jr tells the film-makers.

‘I had tangerines in my knickers,’ says Pauline O'Rourke (right), who is interviewed with her twin sister, Christine Atkinson, in the documentary about Blackpool's fight to get rid of the owners

‘My father created a whole department, scouring message boards full-time so he could sue them,’ Oyston Jr (pictured in 2010) tells the film-makers

‘We felt like medieval peasants, coming up against a king,’ says Tangerine Knight Kevin Quirke, interviewed with his fellow combatant Scott Koudellas inside the tangerine GTI, parked up on Blackpool’s South Shore – one of the film’s many wonderful touches.

Ragozzino lost his job and faced a £150,000 legal suit. Fielding, a solicitor, was told it would cost more than £250,000 to defend himself against Oyston’s legal action. The Oystons forced him to pay them £10,000 in cash and issue a public apology.

Karl Oyston reveals how much he revelled in the war with fans, delighting in the ‘Oyston Out’ personalised number plate his wife bought for Christmas to maintain the mockery. ‘She thought it was highly amusing. Which it was,’ he relates.

Suing elderly Blackpool fans was his father’s idea, he says. ‘But as soon as the board makes a decision, you fight to the death to support it.’

Oyston Snr maintains he was perfectly entitled to pay himself £11m of the Premier League money. ‘Why wouldn’t we? Why shouldn’t we?’ he asks. ‘We own the company. We’d had 25 years of pouring money down the drain without the least prospect of seeing any of it ever again.’

It was Fielding who came up with the game-changing strategy – persuading minority shareholder Valeri Belokon to mount a successful legal challenge against the Oystons, eventually clearing the way for Simon Sadler, a Hong Kong-based financier and Blackpudlian to buy the club.

It’s not been a bed of roses these past few years. An interim club board, formed after Oyston was ousted, included Ben Hatton, later chief operating officer at Aston Villa, former Inter Milan CEO Mike Bolingbroke and Fielding. But a succession of good leaders have left.

Brett Gerrity, a one-time close friend of Sadler who persuaded him to buy the club, resigned in 2023. The two no longer get on. Ben Mansford, respected ex-CEO at Leeds and Barnsley, also unexpectedly left. Former sporting director David Downes was recently made CEO. Amid these comings and goings, Sadler has not appointed a successful manager since Neil Critchley left to assist Steven Gerrard at Aston Villa in 2022.

‘We felt like medieval peasants, coming up against a king,’ says Tangerine Knight Kevin Quirke (right), interviewed with his fellow combatant Scott Coudellas inside the tangerine GTI

Christine Seddon was a leading figure in the fight to rid Blackpool of the Oystons

None of this has affected fans’ views of Sadler, a boyhood Blackpool fan whose investment is still giving the club a top eight budget in League One. He has spent money on upgrades to the stadium and training ground and the team’s playing surface is excellent.

But his own future at Bloomfield Road is in doubt. He is on trial in Hong Kong over accusations of insider dealing linked to his former hedge fund and could face a prison sentence if convicted.

That would mean him failing the EFL Owners’ and Directors’ Test and he would seemingly have to sell. The verdict in that case is expected next February. Sadler, who has pleaded not guilty to the charges, has revealed little of any contingencies he might have made. He is thought to be prepared to sell the club, though only if the buyer will be a true custodian.

‘He’s acutely aware of not putting Blackpool right back where it was with Oyston,’ says one source.

‘The club is so much better and professional than it used to be,' Seddon tells us. ‘But we are short of football business experience. We don’t have a proper board at the moment.

'Hedge fund management – our owner’s world – does not always translate well into football. It’s a steep learning curve.’

Oyston Snr revealed in a recent interview that he wants to buy the club back and gift a majority share to fans. ‘In 2015, we suggested to him that he walk away and leave the club’s assets to the fans,’ says Seddon.

‘He ignored us, yet now he’s suggesting this. These are deluded ramblings. Simon Sadler would not give Oyston the time of day.’

'When I hear some fans complaining about the club, I think: “Have you forgotten? Are your memories quite short?”'

Karl Oyston tells the documentary-makers that he has not spoken to his 92-year-old father since the family’s 32-year ownership of the club ended in 2019. Will he ever see him again, he is asked. ‘No. That ship’s sailed,’ he replies.

Blackpool, backed by a loud, strong away following, fell to a 1-0 defeat at Wimbledon and boss Ian Evatt’s job will be on the line when they face fellow-strugglers Wigan on Saturday, so the film is a particularly timely reminder of how far this club’s fans have come.

‘Yes, we want results to be better,’ Seddon says. ‘But when I hear some complaining about the club, I think: “Have you forgotten? Are your memories quite short?” Our club became an opportunity for people who were dismantling it for their own benefit. There were times when we thought we would lose it altogether.

'But we’re now in a place where we were beginning to believe we would never be. We’re thankful for that.’

The Battle for Blackpool will premiere in the UK on November 21 on Sky Documentaries and streaming service NOW

#1737. New deals for all, Odegaard’s brilliance, assists galore

Good morning! I’ve got to say, if I worked at Arsenal and I wasn’t getting a new contract this international break, I think I’d be taking it pretty personally.

After Monday’s news that both Jurrien Timber and Declan Rice have agreed new deals with the club, Tuesday brought the news that fellow 2023 signing David Raya was next in line, swiftly followed by reports that Riccardo Calafiori will also be handed a new deal, and Piero Hincapie will be getting improved terms, too.

Since the end of the 2024-25 season, there have already been new deals for Gabriel, Myles Lewis-Skelly, Ethan Nwaneri, William Saliba, Bukayo Saka, and, of course, Mikel Arteta. With the latest raft of agreements on top of those, that’s a lot of important people tied down for the next few years.

These deals will mean everyone other than Kai Havertz, Martin Odegaard, Ben White, Mikel Merino, and Kepa is contracted to the club until at least 2029. That’s a nice feeling, isn’t it? There will be some decisions to be made over a couple of those players and whether it’s time to refresh, you’d imagine, but the bulk of the squad should be staying put and continuing to compete together – with a couple of additions supplementing them, of course – for the next couple of years at least.

Of those four (plus Kepa) mentioned above, you’d have to think Odegaard is the next priority when it comes to renewals, given his importance on and off the pitch and his current form.

I was in a bar here in Berlin catching up with a fellow Arsenal fan yesterday evening (hello, if you’re reading!) and they had Norway’s game in Denmark on. It’s fair to say the skipper continued his fine start to the season.

After Norway went two down against the run of play, Odegaard sprung into action. No player had as many touches on the night, and he was involved in all three Norway goals.

He stole the ball for the goal that made it 2-1, which, by the way, we should have a word for. We have the word equaliser for when it goes to 2-2, but we don’t have a word for the goal that shortens the lead. The Germans call it an Anschlusstor – literally a ‘connecting goal’, the goal that means the scores are now just one apart.

Anyway, Odegaard, pressing as he always does, stole the ball from goalkeeper Mads Hermansen, then selflessly left the tap-in for Erling Haaland. He then scored the equaliser, a goal reminiscent of his opening day strike against Coventry if we’re honest: he didn’t hit it well, he got a bit lucky. But: right place, right time and all that.

And, finally, it was Odegaard’s ferociously whipped in free-kick that struck the hand of Joachim Andersen and allowed Haaland to convert from the penalty spot late into added time. If you’ve got a few minutes, you can see the highlights of his performance here – some of the touches are more than worth your time.

A good night’s work, especially after he was suffering with a stomach bug last week.

It wasn’t just the captain in action yesterday, either. Piero Hincapie played just over an hour for Ecuador overnight, there were assists for Gabriel and Bruno Guimaraes as Brazil beat Singapore 7-0 earlier on in the day, and then an assist for Viktor Gyokeres too as Sweden drew with Poland.

That looks like something he’s clearly worked on – getting his body in the way of the defender and, rather than holding the ball up, looking to direct it towards an oncoming runner. His assist for Declan Rice in Munich obviously looked pretty similar, and it’s not something we saw too much of last season.

In fact, I thought I’d have a quick look, and Gyokeres has 13 key passes (a pass that leads a shot from a team-mate) in the Premier League and Champions League this season. He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes. Last season he had a key pass every 104 minutes across those two competitions. It’s hard not to conclude that he’s been working on that side of his game, and these Giroud-esque back-to-goal touches for team-mates are more than welcome.

So, plenty of assists this break. Now we just need to harness that at Newcastle on Saturday and actually have someone to stick the ball in the back of the net at the end of those moves. Thankfully – knock on wood – it seems the players have made it through the break unscathed (there was also another behind-closed-doors appearance for William Saliba – a nod to Tom Canton for that story) and should be raring to go.

Lastly, I want to point you towards Arseblog News, where Andrew A wrote something last night on the death of double-winner Peter Storey, one of just eight players to make over 500 appearances for the club. That first double is such an enormous part of our history wouldn’t have happened without Storey’s nerves of steel in the FA Cup semi-final.

#1735. Gyok stats, KMI nonsense, wrong Bournemouth player linked

Andrew M here after a couple of days ‘off’, but not the kind where you sit in a hammock and have delicious things brought to you. More the kind where you have three stab wounds in your abdomen and a chunk of your insides taken out. If at all possible, I seriously recommend the former to the latter. Anyway, I’m here right now with coffee and painkillers, which I guess is something akin to Arseblog heritage.

The Interlull is over and that’s it now until March. It’s non-stop Arsenal all the way, and all the focus will be on us and what we can produce on the pitch. For those interested in what our players got up to during this break, and what they delivered for their respective nations, Andrew A has a handy round-up over on Arseblog News. Now it’s about keeping everyone as fit as possible, the manager using the squad in the smartest and most effective way he can, and for some of the players who are capable of producing more doing exactly that.

I was quite interested in Lewis’ quick look at Viktor Gyokeres and his key pass metrics from yesterday’s blog: He’s delivering a key pass every 28.4 minutes. Last season he had a key pass every 104 minutes across those two competitions [PL & CL].

I think sample size might be a factor here, because when you look at his xG per 90, it’s 0.05 per 90 in both Premier League and Champions League this season, versus .99 and .76 per 90 last season, but obviously he played more minutes last time out. After 14 appearances this season, he’s rustled up a total of 614 minutes; this time last season his first 14 appearances brought him a cumulative 1200+ minutes. The absence of Kai Havertz was a factor, obviously, but it was probably that early season load that contributed to the injury he picked up against Burnley after a solid first half performance.

The job for Mikel Arteta is to find a way to share those minutes effectively, to have both his strikers scoring and assisting, and to harness some of what Gyokeres has been able to produce for Sweden. It’s often mooted that as a team we need to play to his strengths more, but perhaps these key pass metrics show that the design is more about eliminating some of the weaknesses in his game to make him more effective in the final third for us. Let’s see how it goes.

Meanwhile, the KMI (Key Match Incident) panel have ruled on the Kai Havertz penalty incident against Hull. They ruled 5-0 that the on-field decision was wrong and that VAR, manned that day by Michael Oliver, should have intervened:

Although Havertz is clearly in an offside position, there is a clear and impactful holding action by Mendy before any potential offside offence by Havertz. Given the chronology of events, a penalty should have been awarded. The panel considered the VAR intervention was correct; however, the outcome after the on-field review was considered to be incorrect as a penalty should have been awarded.

I get every day is a learning day for ‘ProRef’, the people whose job it is to know the rules of football but week after week seem to demonstrate in new and inventive ways that they don’t. The question for us as fans is, what are we supposed to do with this? Are we supposed to feel better knowing that they’re owning up to mistakes? It feels a bit like getting run over when you have the green light at a pedestrian crossing, a nearby cop just lets the bloke go, but then later a judge says he should have been stopped and arrested.

Which is all well and good when you’re in a hospital bed in traction with a couple of broken legs and smashed pelvis (I say this only because I remember being in hospital with a bloke who fell under a bus and that’s what happened to him. He was fine though, his mates brought him in loads of joints which he used to share in the smoking room – this was 90s hospital). Which is to say, the damage has been done, the admission the bloke got it wrong in the first place doesn’t really make you feel any better.

From our perspective at least, Martin Odegaard’s winner ensured that decision didn’t turn out to be one which went on to live in infamy – like not drawing the lines for that Brentford goal that time, but it’s still essentially useless. Not least because you just know this weekend or next weekend some other mad thing will happen and they’ll say ‘Oooops! Sorry about that LOL here’s Michael Owen and Howard Webb!’, and some team will lose points because they can’t properly apply the rules of the game to things that happen on the pitch.

Finally for today, we’re being linked with a January move for Bournemouth midfielder Alex Scott. He’s certainly a fine player, but it doesn’t make a lot of sense to me given we already have the best midfield depth in the Premier League, and beyond. Where does he fit with Declan Rice, Bruno Guimaraes, Martin Zubimendi, Mikel Merino, Myles Lewis-Skelly and Martin Odegaard? Perhaps if, for example, Zubi went there’s a case to be made for a replacement, but as it is he’s struggling for minutes anyway, and you don’t pay that kind of money for someone to come in and be peripheral.

Like most of you, if there’s money to be spent in January, I’d much rather see it go on the forward line where I feel like there’s obvious room for improvement and to increase our depth. The left hand side is the obvious place, it’s hard not to worry about the right a little bit with Bukayo Saka’s injury, and the striker conversation is one which is never quite going to go away. So, on that basis, links to Scott don’t really add up for me. Unless Arteta fancies converting him to another left-back. Then it all clicks, but I think there’s one Bournemouth player we’d all rather see arrive.

Right, I’m gonna leave it there for this morning. In terms of a podcast, I’m not quite feeling up to it today, but what we’ll do is make our Patreon preview podcast free and available to everyone tomorrow afternoon. I should be less sore then, and I continue to be blown away by your many emails and messages. Thank you so much, they mean the world.

#1734. Process of Elimination

Over the course of the November international break, news of contract extensions for some of Arsenal’s ‘pillar’ players has begun to filter through. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Piero Hincapie are all reportedly on the verge of new deals, with Riccardo Calafiori’s deal also in the in-tray for Andrea Berta too.

Arsenal have assembled an elite core and it didn’t happen overnight. Back in the summer of 2021, the club enacted a policy of buying players under 24 years old. I always felt like this was the true year zero of the Arteta project. That always felt like the window that built the foundations.

In hindsight, it’s interesting that only Ben White and Martin Odegaard have ‘survived’ since then, with Ramsdale, Tomiyasu, Lokonga and Tavares all having drifted away ever since. Emile Smith Rowe also signed a new contract and took the number 10 shirt that summer and now he is scratching around for minutes at Fulham.

The summer of 2022 saw the arrivals of Gabriel Jesus and Alex Zinchenko, as well as Fabio Vieira. The former pair briefly elevated Arsenal to a new level before becoming quickly obsolete. Vieira was a fairly pricey gamble that didn’t pay off. It was the summer of 2023 that truly established Arsenal among England’s elite. David Raya, Jurrien Timber, Declan Rice and Kai Havertz’s arrivals turned Arsenal from caterpillars to butterflies.

Three of those players are about to sign new contracts. Curiously, we have little to no reporting on whether Kai Havertz is lined up for a new deal as yet. Arsenal are banking on their well assembled core to deliver more silverware as they enter their peak years (Raya is 31 which feels close to peak age for a goalkeeper).

Undoubtedly, there are some players who will drift away in the coming years. Mikel Merino, Martin Zubimendi and Ben White feel unlikely to get new Arsenal contracts at this particular moment in time. (Though these things can and do change). Like Havertz, Odegaard’s deal runs until the summer of 2028 and we have yet to hear rumblings of a new deal.

Odegaard and Havertz have negotiated significant fitness challenges over the last two seasons, which probably explains why they have found themselves lower down Berta’s to do list. Timber has had his own physical challenges too, but he is 25. Havertz and Odegaard are 27. Their next contracts will be their last ‘big’ contracts in terms of wages and their resale value will drop to close to zero if Arsenal tie them down. It makes sense for the club to take its time a little more with both players.

Both are also defining attacking and / or creative players in the Arsenal team. At some point, Arteta is going to have to plot an evolution within this core and it feels like that is more likely to happen in the final third of the pitch than within the core of players who operate behind the ball. Behind the ball, Arsenal are absolutely tip top and have some of the most elite players in the world in their positions.

That is not as true ahead of the ball. Odegaard and Havertz remain, for my money, elite, defining players for Arsenal. For the purposes of this piece; I am going to speculate that Odegaard is going to be offered a new contract given his status in the team and because his role is a little more holistic and he doesn’t solely operate in the final third.

Which leaves us with Havertz. I rate Havertz really highly and believe he is integral to Arsenal’s style, he has the technical quality to play one touch football and the physical quality to act as a release valve and hold the ball up. I can’t think of many forwards who offer both sides of the game to such an extent.

There are several Arsenal attackers I would trade in before Havertz. However, the market doesn’t always bend to your will. Arsenal remain a self sustaining club and in the PSR / SCR era, player trading has never been more important or more voluminous. Keeping money swishing between the cost and revenue columns is a necessity in this environment.

Who you would ideally like to sell and who the market wants to buy are often not the same things. I wouldn’t think twice about selling Eze or Gyokeres before I would sell Kai Havertz. But Eze and Gyokeres will be 29 next summer and even putting aside their age, I don’t think they would command the same fee that Havertz would. Havertz is also on a pretty sizeable salary at the moment and players rarely sign up for anything other than a pay rise, which is a big consideration.

Clearly, the number one impediment to Havertz getting a new deal is his fitness. He is still clearly preferred by the manager to Viktor Gyokeres. I have to say I am surprised (a little unpleasantly) at how quickly the tide of opinion has turned against Havertz. The run he went on very recently that saw him score in the Champions League Final, score the goal that clinched the title against Burnley, a critical goal against Chelsea and the winning goal at Anfield seem to have just bought him absolutely no credit within the fan base, which I find a little surprising.

However, Arsenal need to boost their attacking prowess overall at some point very soon. Like I said, I would consider Havertz a superior player to all of Eze, Gyokeres, Tzolis and Madueke. The squad is well served for numbers in attack; it doesn’t have any gaps in that respect. It has a gap in elite quality.

The key to boosting that might not be ‘who is the least effective player?’ it might be ‘who is the most saleable?’ Sometimes you do just have to cash in your chips on a player to evolve and move forwards. It doesn’t always have to be because the player is obsolete or not good enough. Arsenal have such numbers in midfield that there also isn’t really a route into the team there for Havertz either.

If someone offered £60-70m for Gyokeres or Eze, I would accept it and give Havertz a new contract the next day (assuming he does prove his fitness). But I think those scenarios are unlikely. I am not arguing that we have definitely reached the ‘we must sell Kai’ stage and I will reiterate that, at this moment in time, I consider him a very key player who should pretty much always start when fit.

While he isn’t the most prolific finisher as a centre-forward, crucial goals this season against Chelsea and Liverpool demonstrate his worth. The conversation about moving on only becomes live on condition that the money is used to immediately buy an obviously elite attacker- preferably a centre-forward in that case since that is the gap a Havertz departure would leave.

But I am certain it is a conversation Arteta and Andrea Berta are currently entertaining. Arteta will want to push the level of the team even further and, to fund what that is going to entail, potentially painful sales will have to be made somewhere. The vigour with which the club pursued the sale of Gabriel Martinelli this summer shows the manager has the stomach for that conversation too.

#1732. GdS: Possession vs. directness – key tactical differences between Milan and Frosinone

Ruben Amorim will be up against Massimiliano Alvini tomorrow evening, and as the stats show, they are two very different managers.

As highlighted by Gazzetta dello Sport, there is one interesting stat to highlight to introduce the game. In terms of shots per game, it will be the second-ranked team and against the 17th-ranked team. That in itself won’t raise any eyebrows, but the fact that Milan are the ones in 17th place will.

Read SempreMilan ad-free and get access to exclusive news. Click here for a free trial!

The Rossoneri have mustered a mere 126 shots so far, while Frosinone are quite far ahead at 221. On the flip side, the newly-promoted side have only scored one more goal than Milan (24 vs. 23), which is what makes this game so interesting.

Amorim has made it clear from the start that he wants to dominate each game. That shows in the possession, as Milan are third in Serie A with an average of 59% so far, and they also rank high in terms of passes per game.

The shots are where they fall short, even if they average over two goals per game. There are several reasons for this, but most of it can be attributed to Amorim’s recent arrival and the fact that he has experimented rather extensively.

During today’s presser, he even said that they haven’t done anywhere near enough to enter the penalty box more often, which tends to mean more shots.

In the build-up, for example, the Rossoneri move the ball forward at an average speed of 1.30 meters per second, which is the slowest in Serie A. Alvini’s Frosinone, on the other hand, are great at vertical football: the ball moves toward the opponent’s penalty box at 2.51 meters per second, the best rate in the league.

The Ciociari are masters of rapid counterattacks, so much so that on only 40 occasions have they built plays with ten or more passes. Milan, meanwhile, have 203.

Everything starts in the defence phase for Frosinone. Indeed, they always attempt to win the ball back inside the opponent’s half, which is proven by the index that measures the intensity of pressing in the attacking zone (they are first in Serie A)

Milan? They are eighth, despite being – along with Como – the team to have scored the most goals (4) from a ball recovered while pressing.

The difference between the two is well explained by the so-called “pressed sequences”, that is, the number of actions in open play in which a team manages to interrupt the opponent’s build-up within three passes or less, before the ball goes beyond the halfway line.

On that front, Frosinone are also first (161), while Milan are only 15th (102). Having said all of this, as the pink newspaper concludes, we should expect a spectacular match tomorrow. Both teams will stick to their respective game, which bodes well.

#1731. Some Friday stuff about things

Mikel Arteta’s press conference takes place early this morning, rather than the typical 1.30pm start time. I woke up a bit later than usual, and there’s part of me that wonders if I should wait for it before doing the blog, but then that would make the blog a lot later than usual and I don’t want to disrupt anybody’s routine. Especially on a Friday.

So, the talking points will come later, if there are any talking points. My guesses on questions today:

Also, the bloke from Sky Sports will come to the press conference dressed up as a PS5 controller to ask if the manager is concerned about his players staying up all night to to play Grand Theft Auto 6. Hopefully he requires a firmware update before speaking.

So, in the absence of news and stuff to talk about, I thought I’d point you in the direction of some stuff elsewhere. In a week where we’ve been handing out new contracts all over the place, Phil Costa wonders about the future of Kai Havertz and whether new terms might be on offer for him.

It’s an interesting one because I think it’s clear he’s the manager’s first preference from the two strikers he has available to him. If he was forced to drive deep into the woods and leave one tied to a tree, it’d be Viktor Gyokeres left in the dark forest to try and undo his knots and make his way back to civilisation. But reservations about Kai’s fitness are more than understandable, and while this is a player who has scored big goals for this club since his arrival, there are inconsistencies to his game that can be frustrating.

He turns 28 in June, which is far from over the hill, but it’s then about the cost of a multi-year commitment to a player who, more than likely, you’re probably never going to get much of a return on. Particularly if you have to add to what is already a significant weekly wage packet, even if others will have taken over the mantle of Arsenal’s best-paid player.

My gut feeling is that we’ll probably keep him though, and jokes aside it probably is connected to Gyokeres. The Swedish international feels like the player most expendable of the two in the manager’s mind, and I just can’t really see any scenario when simply Arsenal hang onto both for another season or two, or decide that both can be sold and then replaced at the same time. We sold two left-wingers and a striker this summer and replaced them with one single player, so it’s not as if our track record of augmenting the squad in forward areas would give you much confidence in our ability to undergo sweeping reform.

Thus, some consistency will be necessary, and if push comes to shove, Arteta will sell Gyokeres a hundred times before Havertz once – unless there’s something to do with fitness/injury. The question then is do we renew now, or see where we are next summer? If we add a younger striker to the mix, the benefit of Havertz’s experience isn’t to be underestimated, and then in those final 12 months, if there’s a deal to be done it can be done, and if not, the club have time to consider other options. At that point, he’ll be almost 29, he’ll have options elsewhere if there’s no future at Arsenal.

Of course players want some security when it comes to their contracts and their futures, it might be a case he wants that and that may force the issue one way or the other, but as it stands, it doesn’t seem to be an issue that absolutely has to be a top priority right now (unlike someone like Declan Rice, for example).

For more good reading this morning, Lewis writes about Thomas Frank and Mauricio Pochettino (the big lumpy prick), and the challenges they face with their new clubs. I know I said this on the Arsecast Extra earlier in the week, but I really feel like the latter escapes the scrutiny he deserves for the evil he has perpetrated throughout his career. Manager of Sp*rs, Chelsea and PSG, and now Man Utd, as well as a stint as a national manager during which I thought he thoroughly shamed himself over the Folarin Balogun incident in the World Cup. I know he’s a big mate of Mikel Arteta, but for me he’s up there with the worst of them. A Maroon5 cover of a Phil Collins song brought to life.

Right, I’ll leave it there. As I said yesterday, we’ll have a preview podcast over on Patreon later on, but in the absence of an Arsecast this week we’ll make it available to everyone for free via the usual podcast channels. That should be out after lunch at some time.

#1730. Newcastle a challenge but a good post-Interlull opportunity

Arsenal are back in Premier League action after the Interlull with a trip to face Newcastle away from home. It’s been a difficult place to visit over the years, and we’ve had some unenjoyable encounters – there particularly during Eddie Howe’s tenure. However, Mikel Arteta more or less has a full squad to choose from, and this version of Newcastle under new manager Matthias Jaissle haven’t been at all convincing so far this season.

In terms of the Arsenal team today, Arteta can flip a coin between Ben White and Jurrien Timber, both of whom were on the scoresheet for their countries during the break. My gut feeling is that the Dutchman will start today with White penciled in for Borussia Dortmund in midweek. William Saliba is back after another behind closed doors appearance to build his fitness, but for a game that’s likely to be intense and physical, I can’t see anything other than Ezri Konsa alongside Gabriel today. The Frenchman often needs a game or two to get his rhythm back, and while friendlies are useful, they’re not quite the same as competitive minutes. He too is likely to feature in the Champions League on Tuesday.

In midfield there’s no Martin Zubimendi whose unfortunate run of injuries continues with a hamstring strain picked up playing for Spain against England. The form of Declan Rice and Martin Odegaard means they’re first picks, and then it’s about how the manager views Bruno Guimaraes for a game like this. Even if Newcastle haven’t been great, the pantomime villain in midfield adds a layer of spice that is inevitable after his summer move. If he wants to keep the crowd quiet, he could choose Myles Lewis-Skelly, but he paid £75m for this player for a good reason, and I think we’ll see the Brazilian from the start.

He was a hugely important player for Newcastle, and while I don’t think his departure was among the most contentious we’ve ever seen, he will be a target for their fans, and perhaps for players who know him – and his temper – very well. You’d hope at 28 he’s mature enough to deal with all that, and I’m sure conversations will have been had about not rising to any bait. Arteta has said more than once recently he wants more from this player, where better to give that than his former club?

As for the front three, I think it will be Christos Tzolis and Noni Madueke either side of Kai Havertz. The injury news for Bukayo Saka means he’s going to miss another month, at least, so there’s a big onus on Madueke to continue his recent improved form, but we’ll need him to add end product to the one goal and one assist he’s provided in the league so far. Similarly, Tzolis had a bright-ish start to his Arsenal career, and while the hamstring injury was ill-timed, we need a player who is ostensibly our first choice left winger to start delivering more in terms of assists but especially goals.

Havertz got the winner away to Liverpool, but had frustrating moments at home to Hull. He’s got Viktor Gyokeres on the bench to put some pressure on him, but this front three has some convincing to do and today would be a very good day to produce performances and end product.

Arteta was asked if the atmosphere at St James’ Park isn’t quite what it used to be, because of the way the team has changed and the inconsistent form they’ve suffered so far this campaign. His message was clear:

If that’s the case, it will be even more difficult, because they will be even better prepared, they will have even more necessity to do that, and that’s what we expect. We always expect the best version from the opponent. That’s how we have to prepare for the game, and that’s how we’re going to approach it.

So, there’s no chance he’s letting his team think for a second this might be easier because it’s not the same Newcastle that have caused us problems in recent seasons. Nevertheless, he must have looked at this team and some of the issues they’ve had under their new manager and recognised that this is an opportunity to go there with a settled side of his own in good form and come away with all three points.

It is always a challenge there, but this is a mature Arsenal that should be capable of dealing with a team that has just three wins from thirteen games in all competitions this season. You never take anything for granted, but if we can keep the ball in the early stages, get control, and perhaps even an early goal, the ingredients are there for us to make this a winning start to what is a tricky run of games over the coming weeks. Fingers crossed.

Right, I’ll leave it there for this morning. As ever, we’ll bring you live blog coverage of the game later, as well all the post-game stuff on Arseblog News like the match report, player ratings, manager reaction, quotes round-up and more. There’s also a preview podcast on Patreon if you need something to listen to ahead of kick off. Third-placed Paris FC welcome Angers to the Stade Jean Bouin in Ligue 1 on Sunday, with kick-off at 3pm local time.

Paris FC have scored 12 goals in five home league matches while Angers have conceded 14 in their last five, and that gap in output makes a home win the logical outcome.

Sinayoko decided the last two league wins, with two goals against Monaco and the winner at Auxerre, and an Angers back line without Lefort will have to deal with him for 90 minutes.

The counter-argument is that Angers beat Paris FC 1-0 in August 2025 and held them 0-0 at Jean Bouin in January, and that Rosenior’s side needed until the 63rd minute to break down a 5-4-1 Auxerre.

Those meetings, however, came when Gilli was still in the Paris FC dugout, and this Angers side has been opened up repeatedly at Brest and Marseille and has scored only three goals in five games.

Lopes should keep the margin respectable, but a side that has failed to score in five of 10 league games is more likely to be shut out than to find a way past Kevin Trapp.

Lorient will aim to extend a superb run against their Breton neighbours Rennes, who make the short trip to the Stade du Moustoir on Sunday afternoon.

Sitting 10th in the Ligue 1 table on 15 points from 10 outings (W4, D3, L3), the hosts trail the eighth-placed visitors by a single point, with the Red and Blacks themselves just one adrift of sixth-placed Nice.

A watertight rearguard and a fine record in this derby should leave Dujeux’s men brimming with confidence, particularly after that encouraging success on the road at Le Havre.

However, Rennes carry far greater attacking quality, and Lepaul’s return could help them end a losing streak away from home, even if a share of the spoils looks likelier than a full haul.

Marseille welcome Le Mans to the Stade Velodrome on Sunday evening for round 11 of the 2026-27 Ligue 1 campaign.

In their previous league outing, Les Olympiens claimed a commendable 2-1 victory over Lens at the Stade Bollaert-Delelis, while Les Manceaux scored late against Monaco on home soil to salvage a point.

Having emphatically bounced back from their early season woes, Marseille will be confident that they can beat any opponent they come up against and continue their impressive rise up the table.

Although Le Mans will be desperate to turn around their poor form, we believe the hosts will be far too strong and are backing them to close the gap on the teams above by posting a convincing victory at the Stade Velodrome on Sunday evening.

#1727. Newcastle 2-2 Arsenal: Two points dropped in a game of two halves

In the cold light of day, it’s hard not to look at what happened in the 45th minute of this game as a key moment. Arsenal were 1-0 up, well on top and absolutely deserving of the lead. Newcastle had struggled to exert any kind of control, and we’d already had 9 attempts on goal.

A good move down the left hand side saw Martin Odegaard square perfectly for Noni Madueke who arrived with pace, ready to finish first time. Unfortunately for him and for us, Lewis Hall produced a quite outstanding piece of defending to slide in and block the shot over the bar. That was the difference between Arsenal going in 2-0 up at the break rather than with just the single goal margin.

The lead had come via Eberechi Eze, finishing emphatically after superb work from Kai Havertz to rob the ball and play a deft pass behind the right back. Newcastle’s only chance had come early, a shot from Jacob Murphy that deflected off his own player and drifted wide with David Raya wrong-footed. After that, we bossed the half, with 11 shots in total, 65% possession, but still only that one goal.

It feels redundant to say this is a very, very good Arsenal team, but if we have a weakness, it’s that we don’t turn this kind of domination into more goals. Very often we don’t need to as our defensive solidity and consistency keeps the opposition at bay, but last night we let our standards slip in that regard, and the lack of firepower or being clinical in the final third came home to roost.

It was, very literally, a game of two halves. Newcastle made a triple sub at the break and it would be churlish not to give them credit for the fact it made a positive impact. However, the Arsenal performance was night and day. The opposition upped the energy and intensity, and we made mistakes. Odegaard miskicking a Riccardo Calafiori throw-in provided them the opportunity to equalise, and I do wonder why Harvey Barnes was so free at the back post to slide home for 1-1.

That goal gave them momentum, they caused us problems again and again, some of them of our own making with carelessness and misfortune. Eze got back well to defend in our box but unfortunately slipped, Raya’s clearance was unconvincing and then Gabriel had to boot the ball behind for a corner – from which they made it 2-1. Dan Burn drifted off Jurrien Timber to get a free header, the ball scrambled around a bit before Malick Thiaw poked it over the line to give them the lead. Messy, shambolic defending – not very Arsenal at all.

If we’re being fair, we have to say they could have scored again. David Raya went off with a shoulder injury, Kepa had to make a smart save at the feet of Lewis Miley but why was he one on one with the keeper in the first place? A Joe Willock shot deflected wide in similar fashion to the Murphy one in the first half, and eventually Arteta changed things with Christos Tzolis and Myles Lewis-Skelly coming on for Eze and Bruno Guimaraes who had a quiet return to his former club – bar that first half moment when he almost got enough contact on a fantastic Declan Rice cross but could only put the ball wide from close range.

We did get an equaliser, and very well worked it was too. We played the ball across the back line from right to left, into midfield where Havertz’s smart dummy allowed Odegaard room to drive on and find Madueke. He was Arsenal’s best attacking player last night, he kept trying to make things happen, and while I think the Newcastle keeper will probably have nightmares about letting that shot in, Madueke deserved the goal, and it earned us a point.

It was after the 90th minute when the manager brought on Viktor Gyokeres and Mikel Merino to try and find a winner, the Swede had one shot over the bar from the edge of the box, but had we found another, it would have been a real smash and grab. In the end, the draw was probably a fair result based on how the game played out, and afterwards the manager was unhappy at leaving two points behind:

My feeling is that we have lost two points today. And I say we because we were exceptional in the first half, from the beginning to the end. It should have been two, three or four-nil up, clear. But it wasn’t.

We started to lose duels, we started to lose second balls. We gave the ball away and have really poor circulation balls against their press and their waves. And when that happens, you give them belief.

It’s a pity because the margin should have been, again, much bigger for the level that we’ve shown.

And this is the key for me. It should have been, but it wasn’t, and it too often isn’t. As I said above, our defensive brilliance is fundamental to us winning so many games, but football is a game of variance. You can’t always control everything. On another night Odegaard just puts his foot through that throw in and that first Newcastle goal doesn’t happen. Eze and Raya deal better with that situation and we don’t concede a corner. We can focus on those individual things and say we could and should do better for sure, but you have to allow for some of that over the course of a season. You cannot be perfect for 90+ minutes 38 games in every league campaign.

The ongoing issue for me is our firepower though. I thought generally the front three played pretty well last night, and it’s not as if we missed a glut of chances, but it’s about turning the level of dominance we had in that first half into more goals. This isn’t a one-time issue either. We scored two lovely goals last night but we should have had that game firmly in our grasp at half-time, but in this league a single goal margin is never a sure thing.

The summer was a let-down in an attacking sense, there’s no getting away from that. If we had a forward line that was even close to our midfield and defence in terms of quality and depth, the Premier League would be a cakewalk. I know that’s a bit simplistic, but it’s also a fact. Regardless of what you think of the business, we let goals go to Turkey and Saudi Arabia, and replaced them with a player who has yet to score. Which isn’t to lay the blame at the feet of Tzolis, far from it, but with the squad planning/building that was undertaken.

For me, January becomes increasingly important because the improvement required is obvious, and for a sporting director whose track record looks quite hit and miss as it is, he needs a convincing window or the questions around the job he’s doing will become louder and louder, and for good reason.

The other big issue from yesterday was the injury to David Raya. It didn’t look good at all, and any absence for him would be a huge blow to the team. He’s been the best in the Premier League, and perhaps the best in Europe, for the last 18 months, and inevitably there’s a drop-off when any club is without their first choice keeper for any period of time. That’s another adjustment we’re probably going to have to make, and if it means we’re likely to be less secure and clean sheets are harder to come by, then that issue of scoring goals and being more potent comes into even sharper focus. Let’s keep fingers crossed it’s not as bad as it appears to be.

Right, I’ll leave it there for now. There’s plenty to unpick from this one, so I’ll leave you to it in the Arses. More here tomorrow, including an Arsecast Extra. Until then, have a great Sunday.

#1724. Arsenal teach Chelsea a lesson in how to be champions

This is how champions are supposed to play and, although the Arsenal home support have not seen a team defend their place at the apex of English league football for two decades, they knew it when they saw it.

The chase was on for Mikel Arteta’s team within two minutes when Morgan Rogers, the man who might have moved to Arsenal this summer, put his new club Chelsea in the lead. So unfolded a thrilling 100 minutes of Premier League competition. Arsenal were the better team in terms of ambition and attack even if one could not discount Chelsea until the very last moment.

Others might have crumbled. That Chelsea did not will give Xabi Alonso hope for a team that did not feature the injured Moisés Caicedo and is now without the departed Enzo Fernández. Yet he will also recognise that his childhood friend from San Sebastián in the other dugout has created a side that treated the game, and their place in it, with an urgency that looks different. The first two minutes might have been ragged for Arsenal but after that they did not let the game happen to them.

Morgan Rogers fires Chelsea in front inside TWO minutes! ⚡️ pic.twitter.com/ca8cqnT2Wm

Instead, Arteta’s players drove this contest, and the sequence of chances that came and went was dizzying at times. Their best players scored the two goals. First Kai Havertz, who now has three in four games this season, and then the captain Martin Ødegaard who dispatched what would be the winner.

"A spear through the heart of Chelsea!" Martin Odegaard puts Arsenal in front at the Emirates 🎯 pic.twitter.com/5deEQykjck

Ødegaard looked like the veteran of a title-winning season, and a deep run in the World Cup – an accomplished, shrewd performer in a midfield that was fought over ferociously all afternoon.

As for the game’s defining moment – it would be hard to overlook the feint from Havertz for the winning goal. It deceived the Chelsea players around him and created the channel for Christos Tzolis’s cross to reach Ødegaard. His goal was a close copy, in style and personnel, of the one he scored against Manchester City in the Community Shield but it was crowned by Havertz’s bluff. He shaped to take the ball and let it run under his foot at the last moment.

This was Chelsea’s first defeat in three – leaving only Arsenal and City with nine points from their first three games – although the seven goals conceded is the standout. For all the jet fuel in their attack they keep conceding. This was a much more exacting test than Fulham and Brighton previously, but even so. Alonso has introduced his preferred back three, often a back five, and it is a work in progress.

Arsenal have set the standard in that regard and they were uncompromising again. They did not replicate the errors that led to the Rogers goal and they pushed the limits at all times. Gabriel Magalhães kicked Emi Martínez in the head competing for a ball in the Chelsea area. Myles Lewis-Skelly went after João Pedro. Ben White and Roméo Lavia saw things differently in the first half. This Arsenal team does not shy away from those confrontations in the way their predecessors often did.

In fact, it was notable just how furiously Rogers reacted to Declan Rice when the two England team-mates converged as the Chelsea man charged off to join a late counter-attack. The bad feeling lingered even after the game when Rogers seemed unwilling to forgive. Rice had applied the minimum contact and the maximum cynicism to stop Rogers while the attention of referee Chris Kavanagh was elsewhere.

"He's FUMING Morgan Rogers!" 😳 pic.twitter.com/FciivEedvh

All that ringcraft was one thing, but it should be said that Arsenal were excellent in setting an attacking tempo that will be hell for any team to live with – especially at the Emirates. Havertz is now Arteta’s centre-forward of choice in the absence of a big summer acquisition. Viktor Gyökeres made a late substitute’s appearance – his first minutes of the season. The hierarchy is clear: last season’s great goalscoring hope is now back-up.

“Exceptional” was how Arteta described his team’s response to the early Rogers goal. They had twice failed to clear the ball in their own area when first Maxence Lacroix and then Jorrel Hato created the chance. Rogers’s right foot half-volley was not struck on the full, but it was placed perfectly inside the post with the necessary bounce and skip to mean David Raya never got behind it.

Arteta’s squad runs deep enough that in the closing stages he could relieve his midfield with two Spanish World Cup-winning substitutes – Martín Zubimendi and Mikel Merino. Then there was Noni Madueke on for Bukayo Saka, understudy and first-choice for club and country. This was not Saka’s day in the way it has been in the past, although a very promising shot of his was stopped by Martinez in the first half.

In the pounding that Chelsea took after they went into the lead, Riccardo Calafiori had an equaliser within minutes that was disallowed by VAR on an offside call. The left-back was the third in sequence to try to force the ball over the line from a Rice free-kick. Calafiori was successful, but the second of his team-mates to try, Ezri Konsa, had been offside when he connected.

For the equaliser it was Havertz, accelerating cautiously at first and then full-on with his left foot from the right-side. Ødegaard was well-placed to prevent Lacroix getting close but in truth the challenge never had the force required. Havertz’s shot was not totally convincing but then neither was Martinez’s attempt to save it – every bit as uncertain as Raya for the Chelsea goal.

A precise finish from Kai Havertz and Arsenal are level! 🔴 pic.twitter.com/DqL1MEX4zN

Chelsea had profited from the quick ball out to their right where Calafiori was often out of position in the left-back slot and Pedro Neto could cut in on his left foot. That seemed to be the sacrifice that Arteta was prepared to make in keeping the hammer on Chelsea. If Neto had not struck the post in one such escape in time added on at the end of the first half it might have been different.

Ødegaard struck what would be the winner early in the first half, and although Chelsea fizzed enough in the later stages it always felt as though it was Arsenal’s game. Raya came into his own in the 89th minute when Estêvão, a substitute, cut in from the right and hit a fierce shot that the goalkeeper pushed over. It was close in some ways – and in others not at all.

“It hurts. It hurts because a defeat has to hurt. It has been a very intense game with different moments for everything. We had chances to equalise. In the first half as well a couple of chances. Never happy if you lose.

“After we scored, there were 15-20 minutes where we had to defend too much and we were struggling a bit to get control. We then had better spells with the ball. Overall, it was a very tight, very intense game. We could do better with the second goal to conceded too early. The guys gave everything, tried everything. It has to hurt.

“It is about preparing the best possible way to compete the best possible way. You need to control the overloads on the right side. It is part of the game to have these actions. We continue. It is game three and this is going to be a long, long ride.”

"That's not sustainable" Daniel Sturridge reflects Chelsea's performance after the 2-1 defeat to Arsenal 💭 pic.twitter.com/3EMx88QLA0

"He's not the goalkeeper that won the World Cup" 🏆Jamie Carragher says Emi Martinez is not as quick or sharp as he once was 🧤 pic.twitter.com/SOp4XhoYIr

“I think the worrying thing for everybody else already is that [William] Saliba, who is genuinely world-class arguably, probably the best centre-back in world football, has not played a minute of football so far this season. And it does not look like anyone can score against them.

“There is a massive gulf between both teams; their XIs and the squads. It will take Chelsea a while to get to that level, if they can get there. But I thought Arsenal were fantastic today. We do not normally see Arsenal in these games, end-to-end, because they very rarely go behind. They are so strong defensively they do not need to get involved in those games.

“They still did not look like they were going to give too much away, even though they were bombing forwards and putting so many bodies in the opposition box.”

“It was a massive game with a tough opponent. It was really hard for us; we got there in the end. Our mentality is to keep fighting. Conceding early was not ideal but we reacted really well. We played well in the second half and got our reward. We showed our quality today. The result reflected that.”

“He is a really smart player and moves so well. He takes defenders attention. When he makes the run and I come from behind I am always free. It was a brilliant goal.”

“We knew Arsenal were the better team and they have proven that in this game. The question before today was, how close are Chelsea? And [Xabi] Alonso will be proud of what he has seen. There are obviously improvements to be made, but they gave it a right good go. A lot of very good things and they will be frustrated and disappointed, but they may potentially look back on this game as a good moment rather than as bad as it may feel right now.”

The final whistle is blown at the Emirates and Arsenal maintain their 100% record through three games as they have beaten Chelsea 2-1. They were 1-0 down inside the opening two minutes but goals from Havertz and Odegaard have led them to victory. Chelsea suffer their first competitive defeat under Xabi Alonso.

Pedro’s cross from the right has too much on it and Chavarria cannot head it back across goal. Chelsea’s last chance might have been that Estevao effort which was brilliantly saved by Raya.

That is a stunning save from Raya that may have preserved Arsenal’s victory. Estevao cuts in from the right and curls one towards the top corner. It looks set for the net but somehow Raya makes a fantastic save to deny Estevao.

Chelsea are bringing on Welbeck for Rogers, who is jeered by the Arsenal fans. Welbeck comes on with a note, that he gives to his captain James.

Arsenal have lost a bit of their composure and structure. I suspect that’s why Arteta has turned to Mikel Merino. He screamed at his bench immediately after a messy passage of play, and Merino emerged about 20 seconds later. Merino is very much the “sensible adult” sort of player, who should calm things down. Although he hasn’t yet.

England team-mates Declan Rice and Morgan Rogers were really going at it there. Rogers absolutely furious with Rice tripping him up. “You should have signed for a big club,” sing the Arsenal fans at Rogers...

It has kicked off. Rogers is cynically tripped by Rice but the referee somehow does not see it. Rogers is incensed and marches over to Rice, who has massively got away with one there. Rice knew exactly what he was doing as he deliberately trips Rogers. That is a nasty from Rice, who avoids a booking, yet Rogers is shown a yellow card. That is frankly dreadful refereeing.

"He's FUMING Morgan Rogers!" 😳 pic.twitter.com/FciivEedvh

Estevao is brought on for Chelsea in place of Neto.

Pedro wins a corner off Gabriel out on the left in front of the travelling Chelsea fans. Gusto’s delivery to the back post is caught at the second attempt by Raya.

Double change for Arsenal as Gyokeres and Merino come on for Havertz and Odegaard.

Gusto’s cross from the right is put behind by Konsa for a Chelsea corner out on the right. Neto clips it in but Arsenal head away. James then opts to shoot from range and his effort is blocked by Gabriel. That shot looked to be going on target but Raya may have had it covered anyway.

Rice’s corner from the left is flicked on by Havertz at the near post and the last touch comes off James for another Arsenal corner on the other side. Arsenal take it short and fell to get into the danger zone but do win themselves another corner.

Saka delivers it into a dangerous area and the ball is flicked, looking like it is going into the Chelsea net, but Martinez makes the save whilst on the ground.

Havertz plays a first-time flick into the path of Saka, whose first-time effort looking for the far corner is saved well by Martinez to his right.

Odegaard feeds a clever pass into the Chelsea penalty area to pick out Zubimendi, whose shot is blocked.

Double change for Arsenal as Zubimendi and Hincapie replace Lewis-Skelly and Calafiori.

Palmer gets a shot away from the right side of the box but it is straight at Raya. Chelsea are just starting to wrestle back some momentum.

Gusto has only just come on but has a chance. The ball is laid to him on the edge of the box and he hits it first time but his effort goes over the bar.

The momentum is certainly with Arsenal right now so Xabi Alonso is making a double change. Gusto and Chavarria replace Lavia and Hato. With Gusto coming on for Lavia, Chelsea do not actually have any out-and-out central midfielders on the pitch.

Tzolis is the first Arsenal player into the book today. He is brought down by Lacroix and then demands that the Chelsea defender be booked, waving an imaginary card, and is then shown a yellow himself. Lacroix was also booked for the original foul.

Two former teammates challenge each other as Konsa slides in to make a perfectly-timed challenge on Rogers. The home crowd loved that tackle from Konsa, who won that tackle fair and square.

Chelsea made Odegaard angry about two minutes before that goal. The Arsenal captain, who is a mild-mannered guy, was really unhappy with a tackle by James. They were exchanging some verbals afterwards, before Odegaard then ran away from James to score.

That’s five goals Chelsea have conceded in just over a game-and-a-half since Emi Martinez took over in goal. In fairness, that Odegaard goal wasn’t his fault.

Arsenal were forced to respond when Chelsea scored early but now it is on the visitors to see how they respond after falling behind.

For the first time this afternoon, Arsenal lead and it is a quality goal. Tzolis receives it out on the left and cuts inside onto his right. He plays the ball inside towards Havertz, who is in space on the edge of the Chelsea box. It is really intelligent from Havertz, who dummies it to take away Fofana and allows the ball to run through to Odegaard, who takes one touch before firing past Martinez.

Arsenal just scored the same goal they scored against Manchester City in the Community Shield. Tzolis into Odegaard, low and fast.

As it stands, Manchester City will be the only team with a 100% record after three games.

A few Chelsea players were having a moan at referee Christopher Kavanagh as they went off for half-time. But Alonso’s players need to calm down and keep their cool. There were signs the Blues’ old disciplinary problems could rear their head again with Joao Pedro and Cole Palmer being booked. Romeo Lavia also squared up to Ben White for no real reason. A really enjoyable half of football, even if it was slowed down a little in the last few minutes by a series of niggly fouls. Arsenal are the better team here but Chelsea are definitely dangerous. That Neto shot off the post was evidence of how quickly they can hurt the Arsenal defence.

The first half is brought to an end and it is 1-1 going into the break at the Emirates.

Chelsea hit the post late on in the half. Chelsea counter from inside their own half and Pedro whips a ball first time down the right channel to pick out the run of Neto. The Portuguese forward drives at Gabriel inside the Arsenal box and cuts inside onto his preferred left foot. That left side of the Arsenal defence again. Wide open for Neto to run into the space. Chelsea looking for the early ball every time.

Is Palmer in some trouble? Raya catches a free-kick into his box and gets Arsenal going on the counter with a long ball forward. With Havertz getting away from him, Palmer brings him down and takes the yellow. There was another covering defender, hence why it was just a yellow.

As we approach half-time, there have been 15 shots in total from both sides in the game with nine of those being on target.

Chelsea win it just inside the Arsenal half after good defensive work from Lavia and Pedro then spots Raya off his line. The Chelsea forward therefore opts to shoot from a long way out but drags his effort wide.

Tremendous game at the Emirates. Both teams attacking one another. Chelsea have a lot of space with Pedro Neto on the right and keep using that diagonal ball. Once again, though, they look suspect in defence. The Havertz equaliser could have been stopped twice, but Chelsea defence just did not react. Fofana let Havertz past and Odegaard set a bit of a screen that stopped Lacroix getting close.

Former Chelsea player scores against former Arsenal goalkeeper. Interesting reaction from the Arsenal players to that Havertz goal: most of them ran straight back to their own half. They want to get on with this game. Suggests they can sense Chelsea’s vulnerability.

Against his former club, Havertz gets the equaliser but again there will be an offside check. It appears he is onside as he receives the ball on the right. The goal will not stand. Konsa was offside before Calafiori scored so Chelsea remain 1-0 up.

Hato brings Saka down not far outside the Chelsea penalty area and both Odegaard and Rice are standing over it. Chelsea have just three men in the wall. Rice is going to take...

The two bosses, who have known each other since they were children, share a warm embrace before kick-off.

We are under way at the Emirates. Both sides have 100% records coming into this one but at least one of those will fall today.

Perhaps some early mind games from Arsenal as Chelsea were left waiting in the tunnel for a little while before Arsenal eventually emerged. For Liverpool, Real Madrid, Bayern Munich and Spain, Alonso was one of the finest midfielders of his generation and also played with some of the best midfielders in the world. So the Chelsea manager knows a thing or two about what it takes.

Bukayo Saka has arrived at a career crossroads. We will soon learn whether he is destined to be a good Arsenal player or if he will elevate himself to the level of Premier League, Champions League and England great.

This weekend Saka turns 25, an age when footballers typically enter their peak. Although his legendary status at Arsenal is secure as a title winner, the reaction to the champions’ transfer window suggests there is a general feeling that he can and should produce more to earn “world class” status.

Mikel Arteta is short of such an attacker. He spent the summer investigating whether players of Vinícius Júnior and Julián Alvarez’s calibre might add much-needed stardust to his front three. Failure to secure a big-name forward has led many to conclude that Arsenal’s title defence will be in the mould of their impressive, but cautious 1-0 victory at Aston Villa.

"It's another tough game"Ben White on coming up against Chelsea's front three 🗣️ pic.twitter.com/gfazGGNSA8

It is a relationship that Arteta has previously described as “deeper than just a friendship”. It started with skateboards and sand, as they made the daily journey to the beach to play tennis and football, and continued into their adult lives. When Alonso was playing for Liverpool and Arteta for Everton, there was a time when they both had flats on the fourth floor of the same building in the Albert Dock.

It is extraordinary that these two individuals – born just a few months apart – now find themselves in positions of such significance in English football. But it is not a coincidence. Throughout their lives, they have driven each other forward.

“This kid, he was maybe even crazier than me about football,” Alonso once said of Arteta and their shared childhood. “He was a little bit younger than me and my friends – just a few months maybe. But you know how you always push your ‘little friends’ at that age? Well, we tried, but he was a competitive monster.”

There’s a slight surprise in Chelsea’s line-up with Levi Colwill dropping to the bench and Josh Acheampong coming in. A personal opinion that no one asked for: Arsenal should have signed Joao Pedro last summer, when the Brazilian joined Chelsea for £60m. Arsenal bought Viktor Gyokeres instead, in a deal that could ultimately be more expensive, and there is no doubt which forward offers more to their team. Joao Pedro always seemed to cause problems for Arsenal’s defence when he played against them during his time at Brighton, and he has a flexibility and versatility that would have been perfect for Arteta’s system. Arsenal had twice explored the possibility of signing him over the years. It is surely a source of regret that they never became serious about it. So far this season, Joao Pedro has scored and assisted in both league games. Gyokeres, by contrast, has played zero minutes.

They have just got back under way in the second half on Merseyside and Manchester United have taken the lead against Everton through Bryan Mbeumo. You can follow the action from the Hill Dickinson here.

Will Ezri Konsa come into Arsenal’s starting lineup today? It would be harsh on Cristhian Mosquera, who has been excellent so far this season, but when you pay more than £50m for a ready-made, elite-level centre-back, these are the matches you surely want him for. Mosquera had a slight injury against Aston Villa on Monday night, which may give Arteta the perfect reason to throw his new signing into the side.

Today:Everton 0 Manchester United 0 HTArsenal vs Chelsea 4.30pm

Mikel Arteta insists Arsenal are “better equipped” for success this season, despite falling short in their attempts to add a top-class attacker. Arsenal have allowed four forward players to leave this summer and brought in one, Greece winger Christos Tzolis.

The departures of Gabriel Martinelli, Leandro Trossard, Gabriel Jesus and Ethan Nwaneri (on loan) have raised concerns among supporters that the champions lack firepower. Moves for Morgan Rogers, Vinicius Junior and Julian Alvarez did not come to fruition. Arteta, though, feels Arsenal are stronger now than at the end of last season following a summer in which they added midfielder Bruno Guimarães and defender Ezri Konsa.

“We are better equipped,” said Arteta, who faces Rogers and close friend Xabi Alonso. “We have more players available than the start of last season. We have increased the quality and we have increased the leadership, which is very important.”

Asked specifically about the attack, he added: “Yeah, but that’s another question. We have to prove in that particular position whether we are better or not. Let’s see. We need to play. I don’t like to make assumptions.

“It’s not just the responsibility of those players, it’s the team and the dynamic. We have multiple options to play there with different profiles. It’s human nature. When you talk to people and you ask: ‘Ok, what is on your bucket list?’ Sometimes we forget the reverse bucket list, which are the things you already have that are incredible. It’s very important to value what we have, what we have created together. The ambition is great, but [don’t] lose perspective to what we already have which is amazing.”

Two sides with 100% records meet in a London derby in north London as defending champions Arsenal host Chelsea at the Emirates. Arsenal have wins over Coventry and Aston Villa to their name whilst Chelsea have beaten Fulham and Brighton.

Arsenal could make it three wins from three to start the season, a feat they have only achieved once in the last 21 seasons. They have lost just one of their last 29 Premier League London derbies. Mikel Arteta comes up against his childhood friend Xabi Alonso today.

“Really happy for him [Alonso],” Arteta said. “It is incredible because obviously we have the history we have together, the same with Andoni [Iraola]. To be facing each other at such a level and with the responsibility we have managing some of the top clubs in the country is a really beautiful thing to experience. Now it will be tougher to meet because of the schedule we both have but that friendship will go for many years. We shared some great moments but now it is the competition and when you face each other, you know what happens.”

Chelsea were involved in late drama on transfer deadline day. They were on the verge of signing midfielder Lamine Camara from Monaco only to see that deal fall through at the last minute. After being linked with a move away throughout the summer, Chelsea did in the end sell Enzo Fernandez to Manchester City for a joint Premier League transfer record fee of £125m.

“In football, many things happen and you need to be prepared for everything,” Chelsea boss Alonso said. “With Enzo, we have had conversations, but always with respect for what he has done for the club. It has been great, we are thankful, but it is time to move forward. We take all the decisions together. We are responsible for them, we work together with every decision, big and small.

“We knew that, ultimately, the last goal is to have the best for the team, the best for the squad, the best for daily work here. We want to build a good spirit, a good team, and we have always taken decisions thinking we want to reach that. We have the squad we have. We have a lot of big personalities, players with a lot of quality in all the different positions, different lines and now we are ready to go.”

Arsenal won this fixture 2-1 last season, with William Saliba and Jurrien Timber earning Mikel Arteta’s side three points on their way to the title. Arsenal are unbeaten in their last nine Premier League matches against Chelsea.

Team news from the Emirates to follow shortly.
